title: Hierarchies, Specialization, and the Utilization of Knowledge: Theory and Evidence from the Legal Services Industry
author: Luis Garicano · Thomas N. Hubbard

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source does not assess whether partnership extends competition. It instead reframes partner–associate hierarchy as a means of using specialised knowledge, supported by office-level evidence showing that associate-heavy structures are far from universal. This constructively limits tournament-based explanations rather than directly rejecting them.
qs: 73% of law offices have no associates: these “non-hierarchies” include, for example, single-lawyer offices and offices where there are several lawyers, all of whom are partners.

The last of these, where hierarchies are devices to increase the utilization of knowledge (Garicano 2000), is the basis for the model in Section 3; we discuss here the other three and some empirical implications.

The analysis in this paper informs aspects of these debates that have to do with the division of labor and work flows among knowledge workers; additional research is necessary to analyze its implications when knowledge workers can live in different countries.

kp.k: Hierarchies increase utilization of costly expert knowledge
kp.d: Garicano and Hubbard develop a theoretical explanation of legal-service hierarchies in which knowledge acquisition has a fixed cost independent of subsequent use. Lower-level lawyers handle simpler problems, shielding experts so that acquiring and applying deeper knowledge becomes worthwhile. This is a historical theory and empirical study of legal production, not a claim about AI adoption or its effects.
qs: The driving force in this model is increasing returns associated with the utilization of knowledge: an individual who acquires a piece of knowledge incurs a fixed cost, independent of the knowledge’s subsequent utilization.

Hierarchies enable individuals to increase the utilization of expert knowledge by shielding experts from simple problems and allowing them to specialize in problems they have a comparative advantage in addressing.

kp.k: Market size links specialization, expertise depth, and leverage
kp.d: The model predicts that larger markets reduce uncertainty about the allocation of demand across fields, weakening generalists’ advantage in arbitraging demand fluctuations. More suppliers specialize, making deeper expertise and its deployment through subordinate workers more valuable. The formal predictions are non-decreasing specialization, hierarchical participation, and average managerial leverage, rather than unconditional strict increases.
qs: As the size of the economy increases, aggregate uncertainty about the allocation of demand across fields declines, reducing the value of the arbitrage between fields performed by generalists and increasing equilibrium field specialization.
Individuals become “narrower, but deeper,” and the benefit of leveraging their expertise increases.
On average, managers’ leverage is non-decreasing in the size of the economy.

kp.k: Worker knowledge determines how far experts can leverage
kp.d: In the two-layer model, more knowledgeable workers resolve a greater share of problems before escalation, allowing managers to serve larger teams. Higher returns to solutions can therefore increase both managerial and worker knowledge alongside leverage. This mechanism depends on workers being unable to identify the difficulty of problems they cannot solve; the model abstracts from incentives, dynamics, and differences in individuals’ initial abilities.
qs: We assume that agents cannot determine the difficulty of problems they cannot solve themselves, other than the fact that their solutions lie outside their own expertise.
The time constraints thus imply a one-to-one relationship between workers’ knowledge and the manager’s leverage.
The model focuses on the equilibrium organization of knowledge and abstracts throughout from both incentive considerations and dynamics.

kp.k: Small hierarchies challenge exclusively team-based explanations
kp.d: The 1992 data show that 72.7% of offices had no associates and 11.2% had exactly one; 8.4% of associates were their office’s only associate. Associate-to-partner ratios were generally low. The authors argue that single-associate offices cannot be explained exclusively by theories requiring multiple subordinates, including team monitoring, coordination, and relative-performance tournaments. They acknowledge that monitoring, coordination, and tournament incentives may nevertheless operate elsewhere, and do not claim to test purely contractual theories generally.
qs: In fact, the modal positive number of associates is one.

While it is undoubtedly true that partners monitor and coordinate associates’ work, especially when associates work in teams, lawyers are organized hierarchically even when incentive and coordination problems associated with team production cannot be an issue.
Because our main empirical analysis concerns comparative statics that purely contractual theories do not contemplate, it will not provide evidence either in favor or against this class of theories.

kp.k: Census evidence measures office structures, not actual workflows
kp.d: The main regressions use 11,633 law offices from the 1992 Census of Services, with office-level partner, associate, and field-specialization counts; specialization covers thirteen fields. A hierarchy is operationalized as an office with at least one associate. County employment proxies local market size, with industry and demographic controls. The authors cannot observe who actually works with whom and assume hierarchical boundaries are limited by office boundaries. The evidence establishes cross-sectional patterns consistent with the model rather than directly observing its task-allocation mechanism.
qs: These data are establishment-level data on law offices collected by the Bureau of the Census as part of the 1992 Census of Services.
we do not directly observe which lawyers work with each other.
This limitation of our data forces us to make an assumption about the hierarchies’ boundaries: that they are limited by offices’ boundaries.

kp.k: Survey design excludes incorporated firms from hierarchy analysis
kp.d: The Census classified lawyers in professional service organizations as associates for tax-reporting purposes, preventing identification of their actual partner–associate structure. The hierarchy analysis therefore uses proprietorships and partnerships, representing about two-thirds of industry lawyers, offices, and revenues. Incorporation propensity varies by state and office size; the authors adjust weights for these dimensions and report very similar results with and without adjustment.
qs: If a law firm is organized as a PSO, the data contain no information on the number of lawyers who are partners versus associates – all lawyers are reported to be associate lawyers.

Thus, our analysis of hierarchies uses only firms that are legally organized as proprietorships or partnerships; these firms make up about two-thirds of the industry in terms of lawyers, offices, and revenues.
Our results are very similar when we use these adjusted weights rather than unadjusted weights

kp.k: Larger markets associate with more hierarchical specialization
kp.d: With demand-composition controls, doubling county employment is associated with a 4.3 percentage point increase in lawyers working in hierarchies. The joint distribution shifts principally from generalists outside hierarchies toward specialists inside them: the reported estimates imply about a 40 percentage point increase in the specialist–hierarchy share and about a 35 percentage point decrease in the generalist–non-hierarchy share between very small and very large markets. The authors interpret these associations as consistent with organizational structure varying with human capital.
qs: Its magnitude indicates that doubling market size is associated with a 4.3 percentage point increase in the share of lawyers who work in hierarchies.
As market size increases, there is an increase in the share of lawyers that both field-specialize and work in hierarchies and a corresponding decrease in the share that do neither.

kp.k: Additional associates drive greater hierarchical participation
kp.d: The partner-in-hierarchy share does not significantly increase with market size, whereas doubling market size is associated with a 3.5 percentage point increase in the associate share. Thus, the principal change is greater associate-to-partner leverage among already leveraged partners, not a larger fraction of lawyers becoming such partners. For the distributional analysis, the authors assign zero leverage to associates and partners without associates, and the office associate-to-partner ratio to partners with associates.
qs: The coefficient is 0.051, indicating that doubling local market size is associated with a 3.5 percentage point increase in the share of lawyers who are associates.
In other words, the fraction of lawyers who are leveraged stays constant, but the average leverage among leveraged lawyers increases.

kp.k: Business and individual client segments differ sharply
kp.d: Among 6,262 business-client offices, doubling market size is associated with a 5.6 percentage point increase in hierarchical participation and an 8 percentage point increase in the specialist–hierarchy share. Among 5,371 individual-client offices, specialization increases but the controlled results provide no evidence of increased hierarchical participation. The authors propose, rather than establish, that individual-client work may be sufficiently routine that generalists already know the relevant range of problems, limiting the additional value of vertical specialization.
qs: Its magnitude indicates that doubling local market size is associated with a 5.6 percentage point increase in the share of lawyers working in hierarchies
Within the individual segment, lawyers in larger local markets field-specialize more, but we find no evidence that they are more likely to work in hierarchies once they do so.
It may be the case that the vast majority of individual clients’ legal problems involve routine work from lawyers’ perspective

kp.k: Robustness tests address demand composition and office size
kp.d: Similar patterns appear in relatively small, isolated markets, where the authors find less evidence of market-size-related differences in demand composition. The small-market samples contain 983 business-client offices and 2,355 individual-client offices. Business-segment relationships also persist when controlling for exact office size among two-to-seven-lawyer offices and when examining leverage within larger size categories, except the largest offices. The authors treat these findings as evidence against explanations based solely on unobserved demand differences or firm-size effects.
qs: Our main results thus appear when using only offices in single-county MSAs and non-MSAs.
Conditional on the number of lawyers in the office, lawyers are more likely to work in a hierarchy in larger than smaller local markets.
We therefore conclude that the results discussed above do not just reflect firm size effects.

kp.k: Delegation restrictions weaken specialization’s effect on hierarchy
kp.d: The model predicts that binding limits on lower-level workers’ permissible tasks prevent greater specialization from increasing leverage. The authors connect this to state unauthorized-practice restrictions limiting non-lawyers’ independent advice, representation, and professional judgment. Empirically, market-size relationships are much weaker at the lawyer–non-lawyer boundary than the partner–associate boundary. Table 8 measures the non-lawyer share, notwithstanding an inconsistent description in the surrounding prose; the reported business-segment comparison is an increase from 58% to 62% non-lawyers across very small to very large markets.
qs: Constraints on what lower-level individuals can do therefore limit the degree to which hierarchies can be used to help experts vertically specialize.
These prohibitions are derived from state laws governing unauthorized practice of the law.
Thus, we find that the relationship between local market size and law offices hierarchical organization is much weaker at the lawyer/non-lawyer margin than at the partner/associate margin.

kp.k: Unequal leverage suggests, but does not establish, earnings inequality
kp.d: Business-segment leverage becomes more uneven across lawyers and among partners in hierarchies as market size increases. Controlled quantile-regression coefficients are positive and significant at the 65th, 75th, 85th, and 95th percentiles, generally increasing across percentiles except that the 95th-percentile estimate is below the 85th. Individual-segment coefficients are not statistically significant. The authors suggest corresponding implications for earnings inequality and firm-size distributions, explicitly reserving empirical investigation of those links for future research.
qs: As local market size increases, leverage is distributed more unevenly across lawyers in general, but also when considering just partners in hierarchies.
These patterns may be reflected as well in the distribution of lawyers’ earnings and size distribution of firms.

A goal of future research is to investigate relationships between the leverage distribution and the earnings distribution and between the leverage distribution and the size distribution of firms in this industry.

pts.k: The document makes no concrete claims or predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: Garicano and Hubbard analyse how market size, lawyers’ field specialisation and knowledge utilisation relate to hierarchical organisation. This is a legal-services source, not a cross-domain AI source. Its claims about human knowledge and associate–partner leverage should not be recast as claims about AI, automation or substitution of lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.d: The authors offer an equilibrium model and observational evidence from the 1992 Census of Services concerning law-office organisation. These support their non-AI organisational argument; they do not measure AI capabilities, adoption or effects.

pts.k: There is no AI adoption timeframe or conditional AI prediction.
pts.d: The working paper was published in April 2004 and its principal empirical observations concern 1992. Its model concerns comparative changes in market size rather than a forecast of technological change, and explicitly abstracts from dynamics.

pts.k: No population is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The source studies partners, associates and non-lawyer staff in US law offices, distinguishing business-client and individual-client segments. Its reported differences concern specialisation and hierarchy across market sizes, not AI-induced changes to these roles or clients.
